First impressions of the NVDA Deal.  500BN financing with 6 major credit managers

By far the most notable issue is that NVDA is shifting from direct off balance sheet vendor financing to slightly less direct off balance sheet vendor financing.  The big takeaway is this changes the nature of the counterparty NVDA is taking for its credit backstop.  Prior to today when NVDA helped a compute buyer they got equity or debt from those  buyers in exchange for chip purchases.  

With this vehicle the counterparty NVDA backstops owns the full stack of data center assets including but not limited to chips.  In addition the project managers in the structure are not single data center companies but a portfolio of data center companies. NVDA is taking less concentrated risk than in the past regarding the specific collateral AND the counterparty. 

Let's look at the structure it is very similar to a CDO with third party credit protection built in.   Instead of monoline insurers or GSE's providing the credit backstop NVDA provides that protection.  But remember this structure isn't in itself new financing it's a shift in financing from direct vendor financing to indirect vendor financing. 

How does a trade occur.  A data center company has cash funded from its equity investors and needs chips and the full stack of AI infrastructure stuff and additional leverage.  In the past the data center would buy those assets and buy the chips from NVDA with various forms of deals where the data center faced NVDA directly.  With the new structure the Data center will pay for the chips and all the infrastructure directly.  But put all the assets in the new CDO vehicle and they will retain the "equity tranche".  But they need leverage to buy the full stack of assets.  Private equity and private debt funds would perhaps buy some of the equity tranche and some of the high yield debt tranche (mezz).  In the past those PE and PC funds would lend and co-invest with the data center as counterparty.   With this structure they do the identical thing but invest in tranches of the CDO.  Like all CDO's the senior tranche is where the "power" of the structure lies. In the past high grade bonds or bank loans were needed to provide senior funding. Hyperscalers like goog and orcl etc would issue high grade corporate debt and provide the proceeds to help buy the assets of the data center. The market would accept these bonds because of the credit quality of the issuer.  With this financing CDO they can cut out the middle man.  The high grade asset backed buyer can buy the senior tranche of the new AI CDO having senior exposure to the asset stack and having NVDA asset guarantee and the mezz and equity tranche to absorb any losses before they take a loss. I'm sure the rating agencies will provide high quality ratings to any super senior or senior tranche that this structure spins off.  The mezz and equity tranches and the assets themselves will benefit from any additional access to capital or lower cost that this structure realizes and reduce some of the growth in off balance sheet risk Orcl et al are taking.  

So on the main this is mostly a swap from existing financing to this new version which is pretty irrelevant but on the margin may provide more attractive aggregate cost of financing (provided by all tranche owners preference but particularly senior tranche demand).  

NVDA has probably run out of capacity off balance sheet for concentrated counterparty and asset (its own chips) exposure and so this allows them to extend additional vendor financing in a less direct way.   The net is NVDA running out of capacity is probably as big a signal as them creatively coming up with new capacity but that's hard to judge. 

Hope this helps.

Eric says the biggest mistake investors made in cloud was undersizing the market, and everyone is doing it again with AI:

"In 2014, a really common narrative was AWS is going to eat everything. There's no enterprise opportunity left.

Think about 2014 to now. You have Snowflake, direct competitor to Amazon Redshift, ran on Amazon. You're out-Amazoning Amazon on Amazon. 

Confluent and Elastic and Mongo, Databricks. Then you have the whole app layer. Datadog, $100 billion company.

The view that AWS was gonna eat everything was massively wrong because Azure and GCP were irrelevant then. 

Fast-forward to 2026, you ended up with an oligopoly. Even outside of those big three, you have Cloudflare, which is another $100 billion company.

The biggest mistake everybody made was they just undersized the market.

The market was so big that one vendor could not scale and consume it all. That whole notion right now with what you and I are seeing in AI sure feels like it rhymes.

The takeaway to me is "What if it all works?"

BREAKING: US jobs numbers have now been revised lower in 21 out of the last 30 months by a total of -1.05 million jobs.

This means an average of -35,067 jobs have been revised out of previously reported data each month over this period.

June and May jobs numbers alone were revised down by a total of -103,000, the largest 2-month downward revision since July 2025.

Job market revisions are alarming.

We are witnessing the largest CapEx spending spree in history.

Hyperscalers have committed a record $2.6 trillion in future spending across data center leases and equipment purchases.

This includes leases for data centers and power infrastructure that have not yet commenced, and existing purchase contracts for equipment and services.

These obligations do not appear on company balance sheets and are disclosed only in limited accounting footnotes, despite their enormous size and duration.

Alphabet, $GOOGL, has the largest total, with $811 billion in purchase commitments and $85 billion in leases not yet commenced, bringing its combined obligations to ~$896 billion.

By contrast, Oracle, $ORCL, has committed $32 billion to purchases, but $260 billion to leases that have not yet commenced, the largest lease obligation among the group, bringing its total to ~$292 billion.

The AI buildout has become one of the largest long-term capital commitments in corporate history.

There’s an ENORMOUS opportunity for anyone building onchain AI Agents in the $stonkbrokers (@ClutchMarkets) ecosystem

In December 2024 crypto had a Cambrian explosion of agentic activity, but most of it ended up as chatbots with a parallel token

Since then agents have become far more useful: monitoring live state, simulating transactions and executing bounded onchain actions

The opportunity now is to point them at real work; the trigger for this is that I noticed reference to "Olas agents" in the Tickeryard whitepaper (I'll link below)

Here are 7 ways AI agents could plug into the existing StonkBrokers mechanisms:

1) Cross-chain completion

@TickerYardHQ helps users move an exact asset from one chain to another

An agent could track finality across both networks, complete the destination transaction and manage retries, refunds or recovery when a route stalls

Its first proposed canary does exactly this for one certificate transfer through a pinned adapter

The canary pays zero work reward, but establishes the assignment → execution → receipt model

h/t @jeronxd3

2) Backing + issuer watchtowers

Tokenised stocks introduce more moving parts than a normal bridge

Agents could continuously compare backing, issued supply, pending redemptions, contract roles, issuer restrictions and message progress

If backing diverges or an issuer changes permissions, the agent could alert users and activate a predefined response

3) Mancer execution

@MancerXYZ provides the trading layer for swaps, limit orders and recurring buys

Agents could monitor signed orders, simulate each fill and execute when price, slippage and expiry conditions are satisfied

This opens autonomous DCA, rebalancing and conditional stock strategies without handing assets to a centralised bot

h/t @MichaelHirsch 

4) Stonk protocol maintenance

Agents could monitor StockBooster, Clock In, Broker Box and Opening Bell state, then submit permitted maintenance calls when their conditions are met

@stonkpit would continue supplying the verifiable randomness

The agent would monitor the request, confirm fulfilment and coordinate the downstream action

The Stonk Launcher would still fund and execute the buybacks

h/t @Unclemac 

5) Treasury + recovery operations

Cross-chain routes, representation vaults and protocol treasuries all create operational work

Agents could reconcile balances, detect failed messages, monitor liabilities and activate approved recovery paths

Every action would remain restricted by its target, selector, spending limit, expiry and objective postcondition

The agent can decide when conditions are satisfied while the adapter keeps its actual permissions tightly constrained

6) User-facing portfolio agents

This is where the stack starts to feel like one product

“Move my stock to Robinhood Chain, swap part of it and invest $100 every Monday”

The agent could use TickerYard to move the asset and Mancer to execute the strategy, without the user manually jumping between bridges, wrappers and trading interfaces

This is how agents can take fragmented applications from 20 → 100

7) Agents hiring specialist agents

A Yardkeeper agent could hire specialist price, risk or reconciliation services before completing a job

Budgets, approved providers and acceptable outputs would still be pinned inside the client manifest

None of this has been announced as an Olas integration yet

TickerYard is pre-deployment, its first canary pays zero reward and no external client demand has been proven

The Mancer, StonkBrokers & DERP lanes are logical extensions rather than confirmed integrations

The first wave gave chatbots tokens, but teh next one needs agents that actually complete useful work

StonkBrokers could provide the assets, permissions, jobs and economic rails needed to make that shift a reality

So if you're deep into building agentic systems, I'd recommend paying attention to what @OxSimpleFarmer and the team are building

The next phase of tokenization is not just bringing assets onchain, but turning them into financial products through vaults.

Curated lending vaults have grown more than 50% over the past year to nearly $9 billion. But the category remains dominated by stablecoin lending: roughly four out of five curated vaults run a stablecoin strategy.

That is starting to change as more types of assets move onchain. Some tokenized private credit positions can now be used as collateral to increase exposure. Covered-call vaults can generate income from tokenized gold, while other vaults use stablecoin deposits to finance short-term commodity trades.

The vault performs the same role in each case by packaging the asset and strategy into a product that can be distributed onchain.

That model is already reaching users through familiar apps. Coinbase, Robinhood and Uniswap use vaults behind yield products and many users may never interact directly with the underlying protocol.

Moving this activity onchain does not make asset managers obsolete. Curators still decide where capital goes and which risks are worth taking. As the products become more complex, trust in the curator will matter as much as the code.

Vaults are becoming the way asset management is distributed onchain.

Plasma One aims to become the primary financial account for stablecoin users.

Many people use stablecoins to protect against weakening currencies when dollar banking is hard to access. Their financial activity is often split across exchanges, P2P brokers, wallets and separate card programs.

Plasma One brings savings, everyday spending and free USDT transfers into one account.

Monthly stablecoin card volume rose from roughly $230 million in January 2023 to $1.5 billion in August 2025. P2P stablecoin payments increased only slightly over the same period, from $1.4 billion to $1.6 billion a month.

By August 4, Plasma One had processed $32 million in card volume. Nearly half came in July as monthly volume grew 69% to $15.2 million.

That card activity brings users onto Plasma and gives them a reason to keep more of their money on the network. Each new market requires local payment and compliance infrastructure that other products on Plasma can reuse. Over time, its moat could come from those users and local integrations.

Lots of people asked what we “win” if we beat the Chinese in AI.

Short answer: our economy.

Senator Sanders is effectively proposing the economic equivalent of “defunding the police.” Stripping the tools and speed that let American companies and institutions defend themselves in a rough global neighborhood.

Longer answer:

As AI models and applications grow more powerful, they can discover, circumvent, or disable the software that runs a modern economy. Imagine waking up to widespread banks offline, critical intellectual property (product designs, customer lists, source code) stolen or locked for ransom, and medical and government records compromised or held hostage.

As long as leading U.S. AI labs stay ahead of their Chinese counterparts and continue the practice of giving the latest frontier models to American companies first, so those companies can identify and patch vulnerabilities before adversaries do, we retain a decisive defensive advantage. 

Chinese, Russian, and North Korean actors already conduct persistent cyber attacks against U.S. firms and infrastructure. If we deliberately slow or constrain our own labs while China builds superior offensive AI capabilities aimed at the same systems (banks, payment networks, critical infrastructure, Fedwire), we hand them the means to inflict economic damage that conventional cyber tools cannot match at scale.

In short, falling behind in AI is not merely a technology race we lose. It is an open invitation for adversaries to turn the software layer of the American economy from our singular global advantage into our greatest vulnerability.

@DavidSacks @chamath @Jason @friedberg

On paper, @Uniswap built the better launchpad on Robinhood Chain.

Trading there costs 4x less, the tech is newer, and they've got the biggest distribution in DeFi behind them.

Yet a launchpad called @ponsdotfamily is still outtrading them 3 to 1 on Robinhood.

What's going on?

Why this war matters

This is all happening on @RobinhoodCrypto's own chain, and a lot of people expect Robinhood to be the Solana of next season.

The early numbers back the hype:
• 2.6M+ daily transactions
• 200K+ daily active addresses
• $300M+ in daily DEX volume

Launchpads drive a big chunk of that activity. Everyone watched https://t.co/fuWXRA9LhL print on Solana last cycle, so if Robinhood really is the next home chain, whoever owns its launchpad owns one of the best businesses of the cycle.

The incumbent

Pons wasn't even the first king here.

A launchpad called NOXA dominated the early days until it abruptly stopped issuing tokens on July 11, and Pons absorbed the entire market within days.

At its peak, Pons processed 1.65M trades in a single day, more than half of all transactions on the whole chain.

The challenger

Then @Uniswap decided it wanted the market for itself. What's ironic is Pons is built on Uniswap's own rails, and Uniswap had featured it in their launchpad aggregator just six days before launching @TradePools to compete with it.

This wasn't a quick money grab, it's a solid product:

• Trading costs 0.25% instead of the 1% Pons charges
• Fees compound straight back into each token's locked liquidity
• Every token plugs into Uniswap's entire distribution surface on day one

Hayden Adams framed it as a bet that users "will prefer quality tech and a level playing field."

You'd expect Pools to eat this market inside a week.

The result

And for about 48 hours, it looked like they would. Pools out-launched Pons on day one, 10,506 new tokens against 7,210, and grabbed roughly half of all launchpad volume on the chain.

Then attention shifted back home

Six days in, Pons is back to around $50M a day while Pools sits near $15M, and not one of those ten thousand tokens has crossed a $10M market cap.

Only two have even crossed $1M.

Distribution bought Uniswap a spike in attention, but it couldn't buy retention.

What actually wins

So what's going on?

Follow the money. Run $1M of volume through each platform:

• Pons collects $10,000, hands $7,000 to the token's creator, and burns PONS with most of the rest
• Pools collects $2,500, and the creator gets $500 if they even turned the fee on

A creator earns 14x more per dollar of volume on Pons, and that one number explains everything.

The 1% fee everyone calls extractive is really Pons paying its supply side. Creators shill their coins every day because their income depends on the volume, and holders evangelize because every trade burns PONS.

Uniswap built the perfect product for traders and forgot that traders follow attention instead of creating it.

So Pools got ten thousand tokens from people with zero reason to promote them past hour one, while Pons kept the tokens people actually fight over.

The takeaway

Launchpads are ATTENTION businesses, and the tech is table stakes.

Pools is six days old, so this war isn't over, but winning it means out-paying Pons for the people who bring the crowd, not out-engineering them.

So next time a launchpad war breaks out, skip the feature comparison and look at who's getting paid to fill the room.

"Show me the incentives and I'll show you the outcome"

$CNP (CenterPoint Energy) -- the regulated utility that owns Houston's poles & wires -- just announced $5B in savings for Texas ratepayers driven by data center load growth connecting to their grid via ERCOT Batch Zero.

Here's the math:

>14 GW of data center/AI projects have applied to connect to CNP's grid via ERCOT Batch Zero 
>$5B ÷ 10 years = ~$500M/yr in avoided costs 
>$500M >2.69M residential meters out of 3.02M total electric meters
>Residential portion of savings: ~$175–250M/yr
>$65–95/household/year, or roughly $5–8/month off the average delivery charge

The mechanism: data centers pay demand charges to CNP that absorb fixed infrastructure costs currently socialized across all ratepayers. More large load connecting = smaller per-unit cost for everyone else.

Worth noting: CNP raised this estimate from $4B --> $5B between Q1 and Q2 earnings (April --> July 28) as Batch Zero submissions grew from 10 GW committed to 14 GW eligible. The pipeline now totals 17 GW submitted, meaning the savings could also move higher.

Be careful with labels. 

“I’m a technical trader.” 
“I’m a fundamental trader.” 
“I’m a value investor.” 
“I’m a momentum trader.” 

The moment you label yourself, you start seeing the market through that label and ignoring opportunities that don’t fit inside it.

$AMZN falls 30% to $200 and trades at one of its lowest valuations in years. The value investor says the P/E is still too high. The technical trader says it hasn’t reached his moving average. The momentum trader sees a falling stock and wants nothing to do with it.

Or take $ZIM when it was around $13. It was trading at almost half its cash value, with assets worth multiples of its market cap, yet the stock was well below its 200-day moving average. The fundamental trader sees an opportunity. The technical trader sees a chart he shouldn’t touch.

That’s the trap with labels. Your label becomes your rules, and your rules can make you blind to some of the best opportunities you will ever see.

If you ask me what kind of trader I am, I’m a logician. I’m here to make money. I don’t care if the opportunity comes from fundamentals, technicals, options, sentiment, or something else. If the logic makes sense to me and the opportunity is there, I take it.

Use every tool available to you. Don’t let a label decide what opportunities you’re allowed to see.

Risk management is mostly position sizing. Amazon falls to $200 and you think it’s a great opportunity, but you’re worried it could fall another 30%? Fine. $AMZN falls 30% to $200 and trades at one of its lowest valuations in years. The value investor says the P/E is still too high. The technical trader says it hasn’t reached his moving average. The momentum trader sees a falling stock and wants nothing to do with it.

Or take $ZIM when it was around $13. It was trading at almost half its cash value, with assets worth multiples of its market cap, yet the stock was well below its 200-day moving average. The fundamental trader sees an opportunity. The technical trader sees a chart he shouldn’t touch.

That’s the trap with labels. Your label becomes your rules, and your rules can make you blind to some of the best opportunities you will ever see.

If you ask me what kind of trader I am, I’m a logician. I’m here to make money. I don’t care if the opportunity comes from fundamentals, technicals, options, sentiment, or something else. If the logic makes sense to me and the opportunity is there, I take it.

Use every tool available to you. Don’t let a label decide what opportunities you’re allowed to see.

@Avcomp5 Yes

Risk management is mostly position sizing. Amazon falls to $200 and you think it’s a great opportunity, but you’re worried it could fall another 30%? Fine. Put 5% of your portfolio into it instead of the 20% I recommended. Even if it falls another 30%, you lost only 1.5% of your portfolio. No big deal.

Don’t put some arbitrary stop loss 5% below your entry just because you’re afraid of losing money. Stocks need room to breathe. Manage the risk by managing the size of the position, not by getting stopped out because of normal volatility.

Obviously, if the thesis that made you buy the stock completely breaks, that’s different. Then you get out because the reason you owned it no longer exists.

i’ve often wondered how the Japanese are so good at making beautiful and highly functional physical objects

and beautiful physical spaces which balance the manufactured with the organic, appear simple but are functional, use careful physical composition with appropriate use of negative space, etc.

but any UI they design feels like a dumpster fire to me (as someone with American sensibilities)

after some discussion with ChatGPT, i learned:

- in Western design, as products evolve, designers will often rethink interfaces from first principles to help focus the users on what the believe is important- often resulting in interfaces which appear to be more simple and elegant
- in comparison, the Japanese mindset is often to add capability and not take it away
- some of the legacy is also corporate/bureaucratic in nature, where getting approval to remove things from a UI might require approval from multiple departments who may not agree
- there is also a desire to minimize disruption to customers who may be dependent on existing workflows, so again, add and don’t take away
- kanji has greater information density than many written languages, so culturally it may comport with greater comfort with more detail in user interfaces

fascinating

Adj. EBITDA loss widening to -$17M to -$23M

-------------------------------------------
Why the stock sold off

Three things hit sentiment:

- EPS missed (-$0.08 vs -$0.06 expected) - GAAP opex ballooned to $142M (+34% QoQ) on acquisition integration and Neutron ramp

- Gross margin guide down - Q3 GAAP gross margin guided to 29-31% vs Q2's 36%, driven by acquired lower-margin businesses

- Cash burn accelerating - Q2 FCF was -$110M; management said cash-flow positivity is 18–24 months after Neutron's first successful flight (Neutron to pad Q4 2026, so mid-2028 at earliest)

-------------------------------------------
The bigger story - this was a transformational quarter. Beck is going all-in on vertical integration:

- Acquiring Iridium (~$870M annual revenue, 66-satellite constellation, 2.5M subscribers). Creates a self-launching tier-1 space company - builds, launches, AND operates its own constellation. Closes mid-2027 pending approvals.

- Closed Mynaric (laser comms) and Motiv acquisitions
Signed $1B+ in new contracts in Q2 + post-quarter, including: $397M Space Force Flatellite contract (SB-AMTI - airborne threat tracking from space) 

- $266M Space Force HASTE contract (largest launch contract ever, 18 suborbital missions)
$160M+ in GEO satellite contracts
Neutron on track: 400+ Archimedes hot fires, Stage 1 tank production aligned with Q4 2026 pad delivery
GHOST mobile launch system announced (first pad in Kodiak, Alaska)

-------------------------------------------
Bull case

- Revenue compounding at 60%+ with visibility out years via $2.36B backlog

- Iridium changes the company structurally — moves from launch/hardware into recurring space applications revenue

- $1B+ in new contracts signed in ~3 months shows demand isn't slowing

- Neutron poised to unlock medium-lift in an environment where launch capacity is severely constrained

-------------------------------------------

Bear case / what to watch

- Cash burn is real and won't peak until Neutron flies. ~$1.2B cash gives runway but the clock is ticking

- Iridium integration risk — big acquisition, doesn't close until mid-2027, cultural/operational complexity

- Gross margin compression as lower-margin acquisitions layer in

- At $80 / $50B market cap on $234M quarterly revenue, this is priced for perfection on the 3-5 year story. Any Neutron delay or Iridium stumble hits hard

-------------------------------------------

Bottom line: Q2 was about the strategic transformation, not the quarter itself. 

The Iridium deal, $1B+ in new bookings, and Neutron progress are the real news. The stock sold off on near-term margin compression and cash burn, but the revenue trajectory and backlog growth are undeniable. The trade here is whether Neutron hits its Q4 2026 pad target and whether Iridium closes cleanly.
